title: Hand, foot and mouth disease: comfort and hydration
intro: Hand, foot and mouth disease is a contagious viral illness, most common in young children but also possible in adults. Mouth sores and a hand or foot rash can occur; it is not the same as animal foot-and-mouth disease.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Fever and sore throat may come before spots or blisters. Mouth pain can make drinking difficult. Many cases improve on their own, but the child’s hydration and responsiveness matter more than counting spots.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: A clinician usually recognizes the pattern without routine tests. Seek advice for very young infants, uncertain rash or unusual illness; explain exposure, fluid intake, wet nappies or urination and any immune problems. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Antibiotics do not treat the virus. Ask about age- and weight-appropriate pain relief; do not give aspirin to children. Mouth products have age restrictions, so check before using adult gels. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Offer frequent small drinks and soft cool foods if comfortable; avoid acidic drinks that sting. Wash hands with soap, especially after nappies, and clean shared surfaces. Follow local childcare advice rather than waiting for every blister to vanish. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Very little urine, dry mouth, worsening drowsiness, breathing difficulty, severe headache or stiff neck need urgent advice. Persistent fever, inability to drink or deterioration warrants review rather than assuming every case is harmless.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira offers her child small cool drinks because mouth sores make large meals painful. She watches urine output and alertness rather than forcing food.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben washes hands after changing nappies even after the rash improves, because viral shedding can continue beyond visible symptoms.
